notes: Political parties are not permitted in Andorra in 1970 (first ones founded clandestinely from 1976, legal only in 1993), so no MD 2000 party can be used. Ruling slot 1 holds the General Council of the Valleys under Síndic General Julià Reig i Ribó; coalition slot 2 holds the reformist young notables (catchy 'Els Hereus del 33', with Òscar Ribas Reig). Real institutions fill 13 (the two viguiers), 14 (parish communes), 22 (Sometent), 23 (co-princes: Pompidou and apostolic administrator Ramon Malla i Call). Clandestine Catalan/Spanish organisations active among immigrant workers and exiles fill 4, 5, 18, 19, 21. Islamic slots are tiny immigrant/merchant circles.

0.name: Partit de la Seu
0.text:
The La Seu Faction gathers the officials of the episcopal court at La Seu d'Urgell, a few miles down the Valira, and the Andorran notables whose trade, banks and family ties run south into Franco's Spain. For them the bishop's half of the co-principality is the true anchor of the Valleys, and the Spanish state, Catholic, anti-communist and a friend of Washington, is the model of good order.

They favour firm rule by the co-princes over elected councils, close cooperation with the Guardia Civil against smugglers, Republican exiles and Catalan separatists, and a check on French influence. Their leverage lies in the parish clergy, the episcopal share of justice and police, and the Spanish markets on which Andorra's commerce depends.

1.name: Consell General de les Valls
1.native_full: Consell General de les Valls d'Andorra
1.text:
The General Council of the Valleys, meeting in the Casa de la Vall in Andorra la Vella, is the assembly of twenty-four councillors, four from each of the six parishes, elected by a small electorate of native Andorran men. No political parties are permitted. Since 1960 it has been led by the Síndic General Julià Reig i Ribó, a tobacco industrialist who founded Banca Reig in 1956.

Dominated by old landowning and merchant families, the Council governs by consensus and patronage. It defends the Valleys' medieval privileges, the absence of income tax, the duty-free trade and the tourist and banking boom, while keeping political rights for a native minority. In 1968 it narrowly agreed to give women the vote. Its leverage lies in nationality, land, trade licences and the parishes.

2.name: Els Hereus del 33
2.text:
In 1933 young Andorrans rose against the old Council and won the vote for all Andorran men, until the co-princes restored their authority with French gendarmes. Their heirs in 1970 are younger councillors, businessmen and professionals educated in Barcelona, Toulouse and Switzerland, among them Òscar Ribas Reig, who want the Valleys to govern themselves as a modern state. They backed the petition of some four hundred women for the vote.

They call for a separation of powers, an executive answerable to the Council, written laws on companies and residence, equal political rights for women and an opening to European institutions, all without breaking with the co-princes. Their leverage lies inside the Council, in the business community and among a generation impatient with patriarchal rule.

3.name: Treballadors de les Valls
3.text:
Andorra's boom rests on thousands of Spanish, Portuguese and French workers on building sites, in hotels, shops and the new ski resorts of Soldeu and Pas de la Casa. They now outnumber the native Andorrans several times over, yet they have no vote, no trade union and no right to strike, and depend on employers for their residence permits. Around them stand a few Andorran employees and teachers who share their grievances.

They want a labour code, a minimum wage, a stronger social security fund, decent housing and naturalisation for long-term residents and their children born in the Valleys. Moderate and mostly Catholic, they look to European social democracy rather than revolution. Their leverage lies in their indispensable labour.

4.name: Partit Socialista Unificat de Catalunya
4.text:
The Unified Socialist Party of Catalonia, founded in 1936 and underground since Franco's victory, is the communist party of Catalonia, led by its general secretary Gregorio López Raimundo. Its militants work among Catalan and other Spanish immigrants on Andorra's building sites, and its couriers use the mountain paths from France to bring the party paper Treball and leaflets into the Alt Urgell and the Cerdanya.

The PSUC wants the overthrow of Franco, a democratic Catalonia and workers' commissions in every workplace; in the Valleys it demands rights for immigrant labour. Loyal to the Soviet Union yet critical of the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia, it is the best-organised opposition force in Catalonia. Its leverage lies in its discipline and the workers' commissions.

5.name: Confederación Nacional del Trabajo
5.text:
The anarcho-syndicalist CNT, the great union of pre-war Catalonia, has been outlawed in Spain since 1939, and its exiled leadership, with Federica Montseny among its veterans, sits in Toulouse, a few hours' drive from the Valleys. For three decades smugglers and guides close to the libertarian movement have used Andorra's passes to move militants, money and propaganda across the Pyrenees.

The CNT wants the overthrow of Franco, workers' self-management and the abolition of the state, and distrusts communists as much as notables and bishops. In the Valleys it preaches solidarity among immigrant workers and contempt for the oligarchy of tobacco and banking. Its leverage lies in the networks of mountain guides and the solidarity of the exile.

6.name: Fidels al Manual Digest
6.text:
The Loyalists of the Manual Digest are heads of old farming houses in the high parishes of Canillo, Ordino and La Massana who regard Antoni Fiter i Rossell's Manual Digest of 1748, the compendium of Andorran customs, as the true constitution of the Valleys. They watch with dismay as concrete, tourists, banks and foreign workers transform the land of their ancestors, and they opposed votes for women.

They want the Valleys closed to newcomers, suffrage kept for the heads of household, customary law preserved and French and American consumer culture kept out. Hostile to Paris, to Western modernity and to the money men alike, they would accept any protector who leaves the old order intact. Their leverage lies in rural parishes and ancestral houses.

7.name: Els Prosoviètics
7.text:
The Pro-Soviets are a handful of veteran Spanish communists among the immigrant workers of the Valleys, former guerrillas and civil war fighters who side with General Enrique Líster against Santiago Carrillo. Since the Spanish Communist leadership condemned the Warsaw Pact intervention in Czechoslovakia in 1968, they have accused it of betraying the Soviet Union, and in 1969 the party expelled the pro-Soviet dissidents Eduardo García and Agustín Gómez.

They want an iron-disciplined party, armed struggle against Franco and unconditional loyalty to Moscow, and dream of a people's democracy on the Eastern European model. They despise both Carrillo's moderates and the Andorran notables. Their leverage lies in their discipline, their contacts in Paris and the favour of Soviet bloc embassies.

8.name: Tujjar Jabal Amil
8.text:
The Merchants of Jabal Amil are a few Lebanese Shia traders from the south of Lebanon who have joined Andorra's duty-free trade, selling watches, cameras and transistor radios to French and Spanish shoppers. They belong to a diaspora reaching from West Africa to Latin America, and they follow with pride Imam Musa al-Sadr, chosen in 1969 to head Lebanon's new Supreme Islamic Shia Council.

They favour the advancement of their long-neglected community through schools, commerce and a fair share of power in Beirut, not through revolution. Loyal to their hosts and wary of radical politics, they keep their faith private in Andorra. Their leverage lies in money, family trading networks and good relations with the local merchants.

9.name: Shabab al-Hawza
9.text:
The Youth of the Seminary are two or three young relatives of Andorra's Lebanese traders who studied in the seminaries of Najaf before joining the family shops. In Najaf they heard Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, in exile there since 1965, and read Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr's works on an Islamic economy, and they keep up a correspondence with their teachers.

They reject their elders' commercial quietism and argue that Muslims must be governed by Islamic law under the guidance of the clergy, free from both American and Soviet domination. They regard the Shah and the Arab nationalist regimes as enemies of Islam. In the Valleys they have no following; their leverage lies only in their conviction and their links to Najaf.

10.name: Jama'at al-Bay'a
10.text:
The Community of the Oath gathers Moroccan labourers, many from the Rif and the north, who work on Andorra's building sites and in hotel kitchens alongside Spanish and Portuguese workers. They meet for Friday prayer in a rented room and for the great feasts, keep in touch with the Moroccan consulate in Barcelona, and profess allegiance to King Hassan II as Commander of the Faithful.

They follow the official Maliki Sunni Islam of the Moroccan monarchy, shun politics, distrust both communists and Islamist agitators and defer to the Andorran authorities. They hope for a proper prayer hall and fair treatment from employers. Their leverage lies in their growing numbers and the backing of the Moroccan state.

11.name: Ansar al-Khilafa
11.text:
The Partisans of the Caliphate are a tiny cell of Algerian and Tunisian workers who came to the Valleys from Toulouse and Perpignan and pass around the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani and banned throughout the Arab world. Their contacts are Arab students at French universities who smuggle the literature across the frontier.

They call for a single caliphate uniting all Muslims under Islamic law and reject nationalism, democracy, monarchy and both Cold War blocs. They avoid violence and attention and spend their energy on secret study circles. Their leverage lies only in their dedication and the party's discreet network in Western Europe.

12.name: Usrat al-Wadi
12.text:
The Family of the Valley is a study circle of North African workers and a few students who come up from Barcelona and Toulouse, organised as an usra, the cell of the Muslim Brotherhood. Its members read Hassan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb, executed in Cairo in 1966, and look to the Islamic Centre founded in Geneva by al-Banna's son-in-law Said Ramadan.

The circle teaches that Islam is a complete way of life and that Muslim societies must be renewed through preaching, education and charity rather than coups. It condemns Nasser's persecution of the Brotherhood and the godless ideologies of East and West. Its leverage lies in mutual aid among lonely migrant workers and in the Brotherhood's European networks.

13.name: Els Veguers
13.text:
The two viguiers, one appointed by the French Co-Prince and one by the Bishop of Urgell, are the co-princes' executive power in the Valleys. Together they command the small Andorran police corps, preside over the Tribunal de Corts that judges serious crimes, supervise the parish magistrates and can call out the armed householders of the Sometent. In 1933 it was the co-princes' officials who broke the young reformers' revolt.

Standing above the parishes and balancing French and Spanish interests, the viguiers represent an authority that owes nothing to elections. In a crisis they would govern by co-princely decree, ignore the Council and enforce order in the name of neutrality. Their leverage lies in the police, the courts and the sovereign authority of the co-princes.

14.name: Comuns de les Parròquies
14.text:
Andorra's six parishes, Canillo, Encamp, Ordino, La Massana, Andorra la Vella and Sant Julià de Lòria, are each governed by a comú under two consuls, the true centres of everyday power. The communes own the forests, pastures and high meadows on which ski stations, hotels and roads are now being built, and in the upper parishes they speak for families who still grow tobacco and raise livestock.

The communes defend parish autonomy against both the General Council and the co-princes, communal property, Catholic customs and the farmers' tobacco quotas. They welcome development as long as the land rents and concessions flow into parish coffers. Their leverage lies in land ownership, local loyalty and the parish base of every councillor.

15.name: Els Barons del Tabac
15.text:
The Tobacco Barons are the dynasties whose fortunes were made in tobacco, grown on mountain terraces, processed in factories such as the Reig works at Sant Julià de Lòria and smuggled in vast quantities into Spain and France. They have moved into banking, alongside the Banc Agrícol i Comercial of 1930, Crèdit Andorrà of 1949 and Banca Reig of 1956, and into property and the hotel boom.

They want no direct taxes, discreet banking, unregulated building, cheap foreign labour and quiet tolerance of the smuggling trade by Madrid and Paris. Their money finances parishes, festivals and councillors, and the Síndic General himself is one of them. Their leverage lies in owning most of what is worth owning in the Valleys.

16.name: Botiguers de l'Avinguda Meritxell
16.text:
Every weekend thousands of French and Spanish shoppers stream into Andorra la Vella, Escaldes and Pas de la Casa to buy tobacco, spirits, watches, cameras and textiles free of customs duties. The Shopkeepers of Meritxell Avenue, the main commercial street of the capital, are the hundreds of Andorran traders, many of them modest family firms, who live from this trade and from the tourists it brings.

They want no taxes, no customs, no import quotas and as few regulations as possible, better roads to the frontiers and continued tolerance from Paris and Madrid. Suspicious of both the tobacco barons and reformers who talk of public budgets, they defend small enterprise. Their leverage lies in a trade on which the whole economy depends.

17.name: Guardians del Madriu
17.text:
The Guardians of the Madriu are mountaineers, shepherds, teachers and naturalists who love the Madriu valley, a glacial valley without roads above Escaldes where stone huts and terraced meadows survive as they were centuries ago. They watch with alarm as concrete spreads along the Valira, ski stations climb the slopes of Soldeu and Pas de la Casa, and lakes are harnessed for hydroelectric power.

They want protected areas, building limits in the valleys, clean rivers and respect for the traditional mountain landscape, in step with European Conservation Year 1970. They stand outside both blocs and outside the notables' business. Their leverage lies in the affection of Andorrans for their mountains and the support of Catalan and French hiking clubs.

18.name: Moviment Socialista de Catalunya
18.text:
The Socialist Movement of Catalonia was founded in Toulouse in 1945 by Catalan socialists from the exiled parties of the Republic. Its exile wing, around the teacher Josep Pallach, keeps contacts across the Pyrenees, while an interior wing works clandestinely in Barcelona; both find sympathisers among Catalan employees and teachers who have settled in the Valleys.

The Movement stands for a democratic, socialist and self-governing Catalonia, free trade unions and a European future, rejecting both Franco and Soviet communism. In Andorra it supports political rights for residents and the defence of the Catalan language and culture, the only official language of a sovereign state. Its leverage lies in its intellectuals and its exile networks in southern France.

19.name: Partit Socialista d'Alliberament Nacional dels Països Catalans
19.english: Socialist Party of National Liberation of the Catalan Countries
19.native_full: Partit Socialista d'Alliberament Nacional dels Països Catalans
19.text:
The Socialist Party of National Liberation of the Catalan Countries was founded in 1968 by young militants who broke with the Catalan National Front to combine independence with Marxism. Underground in Spain and active among students, it regards Andorra as the only sovereign fragment of the Catalan Countries, which stretch from Roussillon to Valencia and the Balearic Islands, and it seeks sympathisers in the Valleys.

The party calls for national liberation and socialism for all the Catalan lands, inspired by anti-colonial struggles in Algeria and Vietnam rather than by Moscow. It rejects both the Spanish and the French state, and Andorra's notables as their accomplices. Its leverage lies in young intellectuals and in the symbolic weight of Catalan sovereignty.

20.name: Andorra per als Andorrans
20.text:
Andorra for the Andorrans gives voice to native families who feel swamped by the boom: in barely two decades the population has grown several times over, and Andorran citizens are now a small minority among Spanish, French and Portuguese residents. Shopkeepers, taxi owners and small landlords complain that foreigners take the jobs, the housing and soon the businesses of the Valleys.

They demand strict nationality laws, quotas on foreign workers, licences and property reserved for Andorrans and no political rights for newcomers, however long they stay. They distrust Madrid and Paris equally and speak of Andorran sovereignty with fervour. Their leverage lies in the native electorate, the only one that votes, and its fear of becoming strangers at home.

21.name: Falange Española Tradicionalista y de las JONS
21.english: Traditionalist Spanish Phalanx of the JONS
21.native_full: Falange Española Tradicionalista y de las Juntas de Ofensiva Nacional Sindicalista
21.text:
The FET y de las JONS is the single party of Franco's Spain, the backbone of the Movimiento Nacional, run since October 1969 by Minister-Secretary General Torcuato Fernández-Miranda. Its local chiefs in the Alt Urgell and veterans of Franco's army among the Spanish residents of the Valleys keep watch on the exiles, communists and anarchists who use Andorra as a refuge and a passage.

The Falange stands for Catholic national syndicalism, the unity of Spain and the suppression of reds and separatists. For Andorra it wants close Spanish tutelage, the expulsion of subversives and an end to Catalanist propaganda. Its leverage lies in the Spanish state, the Guardia Civil on the frontier and the dependence of many residents on Spain.

22.name: Sometent
22.text:
Andorra has had no standing army for centuries. Its defence rests on the ancient obligation of every Andorran head of household to keep a firearm and answer the call to arms, organised by parish and called out by the authorities in an emergency. In practice the Sometent appears at ceremonies, but its rifles hang in hundreds of houses.

The militia sees itself as the guardian of the Valleys' independence and neutrality between France and Spain, and of the old rural order. In a crisis its captains could become the arbiters of power, backing the Council, the viguiers or a strong man. Its leverage lies in being the only armed force Andorrans can call their own.

23.name: Coprínceps d'Andorra
23.text:
The co-principality rests on the pareatges of 1278 and 1288 between the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix, whose rights passed to the kings of France and then to the French head of state. Since June 1969 the French Co-Prince is President Georges Pompidou, while the see of Urgell is run by Ramon Malla i Call, Bishop of Lleida, as apostolic administrator after Ramon Iglesias i Navarri stepped down in April 1969.

The co-princes hold sovereignty, legislate by decree, appoint the viguiers and judges, and still receive the medieval tribute of the questia. Most Andorrans see in them the guarantee of independence between France and Spain. Their leverage lies in sovereignty itself and the backing of two neighbouring states.
